details:
**Battle of Thermopylae (480 BCE)**
The famous last stand in which King Leonidas I and 300 Spartans, along with Thespians and other Greek allies, held the narrow coastal pass called the "Hot Gates" against the Persian army of Xerxes I, including his Immortals. After the Persians were shown a way around the pass, the Spartans fought to the death; only a couple of Spartans, such as Aristodemus, who had been sent away with an eye infection, survived.

**Agoge**
Sparta's harsh state education and military training system, which boys entered at about age seven, living in barracks. Trainees were given a single red cloak a year, deliberately underfed and expected to steal food without being caught; the story of a boy who let a hidden stolen fox maul him rather than confess illustrates this. Only the firstborn heirs of the two royal houses were exempt.

**Lycurgus and the Great Rhetra**
The legendary lawgiver credited with Sparta's constitution, the Great Rhetra, which he reportedly received from the Oracle of Delphi. He is said to have created the agoge, the gerousia and the communal mess halls, and to have banned gold and silver coins in favor of iron bars. Plutarch pairs him with Rome's King Numa Pompilius in the Parallel Lives.

**Helots**
The enslaved population, mostly conquered Messenians and Laconians, who farmed Spartan land so that citizens could devote themselves to war. They vastly outnumbered the citizens, which made revolt a constant fear. Free non-citizens living around Sparta were called perioikoi.

**Dual kingship (Agiads and Eurypontids)**
Sparta was always ruled by two kings at once, one from the Agiad house and one from the Eurypontid house, which traced their descent from the legendary twins Eurysthenes and Procles. The kings mainly served as military leaders and priests.

**Gerousia**
Sparta's council of elders: 28 men over the age of 60 plus the two kings, for 30 members. Members were reportedly elected by acclamation, with the candidate who received the loudest shouts from the assembly (the Apella) winning, and the council prepared proposals for the assembly to debate.

**Krypteia**
The "secret service" in which young Spartans who had completed the agoge were sent into the countryside armed with knives to spy on and kill helots, especially any who were out at night or seemed dangerous. It kept the helot population terrorized.

**Ephialtes of Trachis**
The local Greek who betrayed the defenders at Thermopylae by showing the Persians a mountain path around the pass. His name became a byword for traitor in Greek.

**"Molon labe"**
"Come and take them," Leonidas's reported reply when Xerxes demanded that the Spartans lay down their weapons at Thermopylae. It is one of the most famous examples of a terse "laconic" saying.

**Gorgo**
The wife of Leonidas and daughter of King Cleomenes I. Herodotus says that as a child she warned her father against being bribed, and that she later realized a blank wax tablet sent by the exiled king Demaratus held a hidden message under the wax warning of Xerxes' invasion.

**Battle of Leuctra (371 BCE)**
The battle in which Thebes, led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas with the elite Sacred Band, crushed the Spartan army and killed King Cleombrotus I. Epaminondas massed his troops on an unusually deep left wing to strike the Spartan right ("cutting off the snake's head"), and the defeat ended Spartan supremacy in Greece.

**Peloponnesian War, Lysander and Aegospotami**
Sparta led the Peloponnesian League to victory over Athens and its Delian League in the 27-year war (431–404 BCE). Its admiral Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE and then installed the Thirty Tyrants in Athens. Earlier in the war, Spartans trapped on the island of Sphacteria surrendered, and the Spartan general Gylippus helped Syracuse defeat Athens' Sicilian Expedition.

**Ephors**
The five magistrates elected each year who supervised the kings, the agoge and daily government. They could overrule the kings in some matters; for example, the ephor Sthenelaidas pushed for war with Athens despite King Archidamus II urging caution.

**Syssitia**
The communal mess halls where Spartan men ate together. Each citizen had to contribute a fixed share of food from his allotted land (kleros), and failing to pay could cost him his full citizenship.

**Carneia festival and Marathon**
The Carneia was a festival of Apollo during which the Spartans would not march to war. Because of this religious restriction, they waited for the full moon and arrived too late for the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE; the same festival was one reason only a small force was sent to Thermopylae.
